findings.title: Device-limit denial is cached as success
findings.body: tagDeviceUI writes the device cache key before CreateOrUpdateDevice returns. When the store rejects a new device with ErrDeviceLimitReached, that error is returned once, but the key stays cached for the cache TTL (about 29 minutes). The next TagDevice call for the same device ID hits the cache and returns nil, so Anonymous.Authenticate treats the session as allowed and never consults the limit again. The configured device limit therefore blocks only a single request per device, then anonymous access is granted anyway.

findings.title: Device limit check is not atomic with insert
findings.body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active devices and, only if the count is still under deviceLimit, runs a separate INSERT. Those steps are not in one transaction and there is no unique constraint or conditional insert that enforces the cap. Concurrent anonymous logins that all observe count < limit will all insert, so the number of stored devices can exceed the configured limit.

findings.title: Limit error is not an authn error
findings.body: When the device limit is hit, Authenticate returns anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached, a plain fmt.Errorf, instead of an authn error the login pipeline knows how to map. Callers that only special-case authn failures will treat this as an unexpected internal error, so users over the limit can get a 500 (and a leaked "device limit reached" string) rather than a normal anonymous-auth denial.
